That eerily disconcerting statement becomes ominous when you consider that Google has already implemented its new truth algorithm for medical searches, with disturbing consequences. Truth-according-to-Google means that anti-vaccination websites no longer make the cut, despite the fact that recently released federal statistics reveal the risk to children's health posed by vaccines is overwhelmingly greater than that posed by the diseases these medications are formulated to combat.

Does anyone have a link to a source here? My efforts mired me in a sea of propaganda-ridden anti-vaccine opinion sites.

Still, to cry and claim that this is censorship is akin to crying and claiming that the popularity sorting algorithm is censorship because it doesn't yield a selective random sample of hits to remove the effects of disproportionate website popularity. Defending google leaves a nasty taste in my mouth, but without understanding the full context of this enhanced search algorithm I can only make my own opinion.

The new algorithm claims to be based on the truth value of specific statements, as defined by a knowledge base created by Google. All told, it sounds like a good system. The biggest problem is that the algorithm is doing some of the filtering that a person should be doing for themselves. When I search for material using a search engine, I take it on myself to assess what ideas are being presented to me by each result, as well as what motivations the source might have for providing me with a biased view. It's unlikely that I'll stop doing this in light of a truthfulness-weighted results screen, but I feel that biased manipulation of the knowledge base itself could filter certain results completely from the public eye. Think for a moment of intentionally setting the knowledge base up such that the fact that "the holocaust never happened" were reinforced. It may be a leap of capability here, but if it's even possible to skew the system's outputs towards one desired truth or agenda over another, it would be a significant blow to the functionality of the service as a search engine.

And perhaps that is what they want. I use google to find information that will inform my decisions, not to make my decisions for me. If their end game is to attempt to exert extra influence and remove some portion of my agency from that decision making process, I will gladly pass on using a truth-weighted search algorithm. I would still be hesitant to call this censorship. It's a paradigm shift in the functionality of google as a whole, from search engine to decision engine. I do just fine being the only decision engine in my life, thank you very much, and will gladly find another tool to gather information if I can't get it without somebody else's brand of analyses attached.
